question.prompt: Why might the nearby wall complicate the courtyard comparison?

options.text: it proves the paving is cooler every day
It could warm the mat independently of surface colour
it prevents any thermometer from working

question.explanation: The mat is near a warm wall, while the paving has a breeze. These unequal conditions could contribute to the difference, so colour is not isolated as the sole cause.

stimulus.title: A cooler courtyard
stimulus.body:
The following account describes a fictional school investigation. Students wanted to know whether two courtyard surfaces warmed differently in sunlight. They placed identical thermometers on a dark rubber mat and pale paving at 10 am. Both surfaces began at 19 degrees. At noon the mat read 34 degrees and the paving 28 degrees. At 2 pm a cloud covered the courtyard; both readings fell.

One pupil proposed replacing every dark surface immediately. The teacher asked whether one afternoon could settle the decision. The mat lay near a warm wall, while the paving was exposed to a light breeze. The students had measured temperature on the surfaces, not the air where people walked.

For a second trial they planned to exchange the thermometers, measure several days and choose locations equally sheltered from wind. They would also compare the cost and durability of possible replacements. Their first results were useful: they provided a reason to investigate further. They did not yet provide a complete purchasing plan.

workedSolution: The mat is near a warm wall, while the paving has a breeze.
These unequal conditions could contribute to the difference, so colour is not isolated as the sole cause.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: What does Ruth mainly request in her letter about the vacant block?

options.text: an immediate permanent ban on cars

question.explanation: Her opening request is a small community garden trial for one year. The rest of the letter supports and limits that request rather than asking for permanent exclusion of cars.

stimulus.title: Letter about the vacant block
stimulus.body:
Dear councillors,

Before the vacant block beside the library becomes a car park, please trial a small community garden there for one year. The soil need not be dug: raised containers could stand above the ground while a soil assessment is completed. A local group has offered containers and volunteers, although water and insurance would still cost money.

I understand the concern about parking. On market Saturdays, visitors sometimes circle the block twice. But the proposed car park would provide only twelve spaces, and the market operates just twice a month. A garden could support weekly classes and a shaded place to meet on other days.

A trial would not remove every uncertainty. Volunteers may lose interest, and containers need summer watering. That is why I suggest publishing costs and attendance after six months, with a clear decision at the end of the year. If the trial fails, the containers can be moved. Let us choose using local evidence rather than assuming either project must be permanent from its first day.

Yours sincerely,
Ruth Ellis

workedSolution: Her opening request is a small community garden trial for one year.
The rest of the letter supports and limits that request rather than asking for permanent exclusion of cars.

stimulus.title: Night at the jetty
stimulus.body:
The jetty combs the dark with wooden teeth.
A rope knocks twice against a sleeping boat.
Across the bay, a window holds its breath;
then someone draws a curtain on its light.

I came to see the boats return like stars,
each yellow lamp a promise moving home.
But now the tide has folded up the sand,
and all the fishing boats are tied and still.

My grandfather once knew them by their sounds:
the gruff old engine, and the bell that skipped.
I cannot name a single boat by ear.
I count the knocks until the rope falls quiet.

At last I turn. Behind me, in the dark,
the water keeps a language I am learning.

workedSolution: The jetty is described through a comb-and-teeth image.
The image maps the structure's repeated wooden parts onto teeth; it does not introduce a literal animal.
